phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial plosive [b], short open-mid back unrounded vowel [ʊ], and alveolar nasal [n]; the first syllable carries stress.
Voiced postalveolar affricate [dʒ] (like English 'j'), near-close near-front unrounded vowel [ɪ], and alveolar lateral approximant [l].

pronunciation.approximation: 'BUN-jil' — stress the first syllable; the 'j' is the 'j' of 'jump', and the final vowel is short like the 'i' in 'kit'.

pronunciation.note: The name Bunjil is a conventional Latin transcription of an Aboriginal theonym. The PuniCodex restoration capitalises the first letter, giving the standard proper-name form. Because no diacritic or distinctive letter is added, the ASCII string 'bunjil' already encodes the conventional spelling; the name is therefore Tier 2.

domains.title: Creator Eaglehawk
domains.subtitle: Sky Ancestor, Law-Giver, and Moiety Founder
domains.lead: Bunjil is the wedge-tailed eaglehawk made ancestor of the Kulin nations of central Victoria. In the Dreaming he shaped the mountains, rivers, plants, animals, and the laws by which people should live. He is one of two moiety ancestors, paired with Waang the crow, and after his work on earth he was lifted into the sky, where he remains as the star Altair.

cards.name: Creator of Country
cards.desc: He shaped the land, water, flora, and fauna of south-eastern Australia, and established the order of the living world.

cards.name: Sky Ancestor
cards.desc: After creation he ascended to the sky and became the star Altair; his two wives became the black swans beside him.

cards.name: Law-Giver
cards.desc: He gave the Kulin peoples their social and ecological laws, including the obligation to care for Country and each other.

cards.name: Moiety Founder
cards.desc: As the eaglehawk ancestor he heads one of the Kulin moieties, balanced by Waang the crow on the other side.

symbols.name: Wedge-tailed eagle
symbols.meaning: The living form of Bunjil and the largest bird of prey in Australia; a sign of creative power and watchful authority

symbols.name: Spear
symbols.meaning: The instrument with which Bunjil commanded the rising sea to stop, and a mark of law-giving authority

symbols.name: Black swan
symbols.meaning: Bunjil's two wives, who became the stars flanking Altair after his ascent

symbols.name: Rainbow
symbols.meaning: His son Binbeal, the rainbow spirit, who continues the creative lineage in the sky

mythology.lead: Bunjil's stories belong to the Dreaming of the Kulin nations — the Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung, Wathaurong, and their neighbors — recorded by A. W. Howitt, Aldo Massola, and the communities themselves. They explain how Country was made, how law was given, and how the creator withdrew into the sky so that he might continue to watch over the world.

myths.title: Shaping the Land and the Law
myths.text: In the Dreaming, Bunjil travelled across what is now central Victoria and shaped Country into its living form: he raised the mountains, traced the courses of the rivers, named the plants and animals, and taught each where it belonged. Then he did what a mere landscape-maker would not: he gave law. The Kulin peoples remember him establishing the rules of kinship and marriage, the obligations between clans, and the duties each people owes to its Country — seasonal burning, careful taking, respect for the places where spirit beings remain. His two wives, the black swans, and his son Binbeal the rainbow accompanied the work. Crucially, the stories insist that Country and law were made together: the mountains are not scenery but scripture, and the river's bends are not geography but instruction. (Howitt 1904; Massola 1968) The tradition encodes a complete environmental philosophy — creation, tenure, and responsibility in a single narrative.

myths.title: The Sea That Would Not Stop Rising
myths.text: In the telling recorded from Boonwurrung elder Carolyn Briggs, the Kulin nations fell into conflict and began to neglect family and Country, and the sea rose in anger and would not stop. The people gathered and asked Bunjil to intervene. He agreed — but on a condition: they must change their ways and return to the law. He walked to the water's edge, raised his spear, and commanded the sea to stop, and the sea stopped. (Briggs, 'Boon Wurrung Story', Yarra Healing 2000) The story is told as a moral charter, but it carries what may be a far older memory: at the end of the last Ice Age, rising seas flooded the Bassian Plain and cut Tasmania from the mainland — an inundation the ancestors of the Kulin peoples witnessed over generations, and which Australia's oral traditions are now famous for preserving with geological accuracy. The myth's force lies in its bargain: the sea keeps its bounds only while the people keep their obligations — a covenant, not a one-time miracle.

myths.title: Lifted into the Sky
myths.text: When his work was finished, Bunjil called his family together and asked Waang, the crow, to release the winds — which Waang kept tied in skin bags — so that they might all be carried to the sky. Waang opened the whirlwind, and the wind lifted Bunjil and his wives and son upward. Bunjil became the bright star Altair; his two wives, the black swans, became the stars on either side; and some tellings say he departed from the island of Deen Maar, off the coast of what is now south-western Victoria, which remains a sacred place of the Gunditjmara and Eastern Maar peoples. (Howitt 1904; Mudrooroo 1994; NIAA, Deen Maar Indigenous Protected Area) The departure is not an abandonment: the eaglehawk still circles above Country, and the star still marks the season. The creator withdrew so that the creation could belong to the people — and he stayed close enough to watch what they do with it.

myths.title: Bunjil's Shelter
myths.text: In Gariwerd — the country now known as the Grampians — Bunjil took shelter in a cave in the Black Range, and there, in red ochre, his image was painted: the creator figure flanked by two dingoes, gazing out over the valley. The site known as Bunjil's Shelter is one of the most important Aboriginal rock-art places in Victoria, protected under the Aboriginal Heritage Act 2006 and visited only under the protocols its Traditional Owners set. It is not treated as a relic of a finished religion. For the Jardwadjali and Djab Wurrung peoples, and for the wider Kulin community, the shelter is a place where the ancestor's presence is understood to remain — a working site of memory, education, and obligation, cared for rather than merely conserved. (Parks Victoria 2009) The painting turns myth into address: whoever stands before it is standing where the creator once stood, being looked at by the one who is supposed to be watched for.

lore.syncretism: Bunjil is not a solitary deity but one half of a Kulin social and cosmological pair. The eaglehawk moiety, headed by Bunjil, is balanced by the crow moiety, headed by Waang — a pairing that structures kinship, marriage, and ritual obligation across the Kulin nations, so that every person belongs to one ancestor's side and marries into the other. Different clans preserve different episodes: the Woiwurrung stress the sky ascent and Altair, the Boonwurrung remember the rising sea, and the peoples of Gariweld keep the place-based accounts tied to Bunjil's Shelter. In the colonial period the name was recorded under many spellings — Winjeel, Wingeel, Pundjel, Bunjel — reflecting dialect variation and the difficulty of rendering Kulin phonology in English orthography; several survive in Victorian place names.
lore.culturalLegacy: Bunjil remains a powerful and public symbol of Aboriginal Victoria. Bunjil's Shelter in the Black Range Scenic Reserve is a protected cultural site and a focus of education and careful tourism. Melbourne's skyline carries his name and form: Bruce Armstrong's monumental eagle sculpture Bunjil (2002) rises from Wurundjeri Way in the Docklands, and Bunjil Place in Narre Warren carries the name into the suburbs. For the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung, Boonwurrung, and other Kulin communities, Bunjil is not only an ancestral figure but a living authority in Welcome to Country ceremonies, land-care work, language revival, and the ongoing negotiation of recognition and reconciliation — the creator whose law still describes how Country should be held.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Bunjil teaches that creation is not a single event but a continuing responsibility. He did not make the land and depart; he shaped it, gave it law, and then withdrew into the sky so that he could go on watching. The eaglehawk's eye is still understood to be turned toward Country.

For non-Indigenous visitors, Bunjil is an invitation to understand 'Country' not as real estate but as a living inheritance — a place that includes people, animals, plants, water, sky, and story, all held together by obligations that precede the colony by tens of thousands of years. The name Bunjil, even in its simple Latin transcription, carries that whole relationship. To restore the capital is a small act; to remember what it names is the larger one — and the first of the obligations it describes.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Kulin languages were traditionally oral, and Bunjil has no original alphabetic script. The name survives in Latin transcription made by early settlers and anthropologists. PuniCodex therefore treats Bunjil as the scholarly citation form and bunjil as the DNS compromise. The restoration adds only the capital initial; the absence of diacritics or special letters places the name in Tier 2, not because the figure is less significant, but because the ASCII form already carries the conventional spelling.

lore.archaeology: The principal material site associated with Bunjil is Bunjil's Shelter, a rock-art shelter in the Black Range Scenic Reserve within Gariwerd (the Grampians region), Victoria, where a red-ochre painting depicts the creator figure flanked by two dingoes. The site is protected under the Aboriginal Heritage Act 2006 and is managed with Traditional Owner input. Textual witnesses include A. W. Howitt's ethnographic notes, Aldo Massola's 1968 compilation of south-eastern traditions, and contemporary community publications by Kulin educators and language custodians — together forming an unusually well-documented record of a living tradition.

etymology.derivation: Theonym recorded from the Kulin nations of central Victoria, denoting the wedge-tailed eaglehawk creator ancestor. Early colonial collectors produced variant spellings (Winjeel, Wingeel, Pundjel, Bunjel) as they adapted Aboriginal phonology to English orthography.

nameVariations.note: Conventional modern spelling used by Kulin communities, Victorian institutions, and the Aboriginal Heritage Register.
Common alternative spelling reflecting the same pronunciation.
Early colonial spellings recorded by Daniel Bunce and others, now preserved in place names such as Wingeel near Geelong.
Variants appearing in nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century ethnographic literature.
ASCII domain compromise: all lowercase, losing the proper-name capitalisation but retaining the conventional letters.
